title: The Space Inside the Jar
hookLine: an empty room after moving day, and a jar worth staring into
carry: the self is like the space in a jar
tomorrow: if worship isn't the flowers, what is it? the book's last page says.

cards: Moving day leaves a particular sound. Footsteps in a room with no rugs, no couch, no pictures: every step echoes.
The eyes go hunting for something to land on and find only bare walls and the pale square where a frame used to hang. It's easy to hurry past a room like that.
So why would a sacred book tell you to stop and stare into an empty jar? Because in the Vijnana Bhairava, the empty part is the point.

teach.h: THE SKY, THE JAR, THE BODY.
teach.b: Several of the doors Bhairava gave the Goddess are built out of space, what Sanskrit calls akasha. One says: fix your gaze on the open sky, clear of clouds, without moving it, and let the mind take on the sky's stillness.
Another takes a jar. Look at the space inside it, and leave the walls out of your attention. As the walls drop away, the text says, the mind dissolves into that space.
A third turns inward: feel your own body as empty, like the sky. Notice the reversal. The walls are what anyone would call the jar.

teach.h: THE EMPTY PART HOLDS THE WATER.
teach.b: This practice says the part that holds the water is the empty part. And the jar is one of the oldest pictures in Hindu thought.
Gaudapada, an early teacher of Advaita Vedanta, used it for the biggest teaching of the Upanishads: the self in each person, the atman, is not finally separate from Brahman, the one reality.
The space inside a pot seems to be its own small space, he says.

teach.h: GAUDAPADA: BREAK THE POT, ONE SPACE.
teach.b: Break the pot, and that space was never anything but the one great space.
So with the self in each body: it looks walled in, but it is the one.

teach.h: THE SELF IS LIKE SPACE IN A JAR.
teach.b: Two schools with real differences, Shaiva and Vedanta, reach for the same jar. So the practice isn't forcing the head empty.
It's noticing the openness that was holding everything all along, even in a room full of boxes, and that the walls never cut it off.

how: Practitioners of the Vijnana Bhairava's space dharanas gaze at a clear sky or at the space inside a vessel, letting the gaze rest on the openness rather than on any object.

games.why: Gaudapada used the pot to teach that atman isn't finally separate from Brahman; the Vijnana Bhairava has you rest on the space inside the jar.

practice: Pick up an empty cup or bowl, or any empty container near you. Feel its weight in your hands, then look into it: not at the rim or the walls, but at the space inside.

Let your gaze go soft there, and when a thought comes, let it cross like a bird and come back to the open space in the cup. If there's no cup nearby, cup your two hands together and look into the space they hold.

wordCard.voice: The Vijnana Bhairava: a book of doors. Today's door is made of space: the sky, the jar, and the self that was never walled off from the whole.

orig.note: Sanskrit akasha, space or sky: in these practices, a picture of awareness.

carryVoice: One line to keep: the self is like the space in a jar, never walled off from the whole. That's today.
